title: Investor Grievances and Arbitration
big_picture: When something goes wrong with a trade, the investor climbs a ladder: first the broker (21 days to fix it), then SEBI's SCORES where the exchange and then SEBI review it, and alongside that SMART ODR, where the exchange tries to settle, a conciliator mediates, and finally an arbitrator decides. If the broker itself collapses, the exchange's Investor Protection Fund pays genuine claims. This chapter is the map of that ladder and the clock running at every rung.
exam_focus: The 21-day rule everywhere: broker redressal, SCORES ATR, MII review in ODR, conciliation (plus max 10 days)
SCORES windows: 1 year to lodge, 15 days to seek each review, 10 days for the exchange's revised ATR; SCORES 2.0 from April 01, 2024
Arbitration thresholds: sole arbitrator up to ₹30 lakh, three-member tribunal above; document-only up to ₹1 lakh; award in 30 (+30) days
Money rules on brokers: 100% deposit of admissible claim before arbitration or a challenge; up to ₹5 lakh released to investor; award paid in 15 days; Section 34 intention in 7 days
What SCORES will not take (sub-judice, other regulators, unlisted/delisted companies, anonymous, price grievances)
IPF: set up by exchanges (1985 notification), 1% of listing fees, 70% of income ploughed back, no speculative claims, 3-year civil-dispute rule; ISF gets 20% of listing fees
Investor Charter timelines and ISC facilities (4 metros, 4 newspapers)

blocks.text: The chapter opens with a line the exam loves: investors are the backbone of the securities market. Protecting them from any wrongdoing, intentional or not, is paramount for intermediaries, exchanges and regulators.

An investor's grievance can be against (a) the intermediary/broking firm they trade through, or (b) the company whose shares they hold. This chapter is the map of where they go, in what order, and how fast each party must respond.

Grievances are handled at three levels: the trading member, the stock exchange and the regulator (SEBI, via SCORES). Alongside runs SMART ODR (online conciliation and arbitration). You always start at the bottom rung, and every rung has a clock.

items.title: Broker
items.text: Complain to the compliance officer / grievance e-mail ID. Redressal within 21 calendar days.

items.title: SCORES
items.text: Lodge within 1 year of the cause of action. Auto-routed to the broker, who files an ATR within 21 calendar days.

items.title: First review: stock exchange
items.text: Ask within 15 days of the ATR; the exchange (Designated Body) gives a revised ATR within 10 days.

items.title: Second review: SEBI
items.text: Ask within 15 days of the exchange's ATR. Closed only when SEBI disposes of it.

items.title: SMART ODR (any time after step 1)
items.text: MII review, then conciliation, then online arbitration; finally a court challenge under Section 34.

blocks.text: Approaching the entity first is mandatory. 'The investor can file directly on SCORES/ODR without approaching the broker' is a wrong option.

blocks.text: The 21-15-10 rhythm: 21 days for whoever must act (broker, ATR, MII, conciliator), 15 days for the investor to ask for review, 10 days for the exchange to re-answer.

sections.title: Grievance handling at the trading member level

blocks.text: Every broking firm has a designated cell/person for grievances, resolved at branch or firm level. Brokers must designate an exclusive e-mail ID of the grievance redressal division/compliance officer and display it on their website, pamphlets and advertisements.

Every broker and AP office displays Exhibit 7.1, a ladder in itself: compliance officer, then CEO/Partner/Proprietor, then the exchange (BSE, NSE, MSEI) or depository (CDSL, NSDL), then SEBI's SCORES (scores.sebi.gov.in) and toll-free helpline 1800 22 7575 / 1800 266 7575.

The broker must endeavour to redress grievances within 21 calendar days and keep records of complaints received and redressed. The Investor Charter for Stock Brokers (SEBI circular, February 21, 2025) sets out services, investor rights, broker activities with timelines, DOs and DON'Ts and the redressal mechanism. Brokers bring it to existing and new clients via website, office display, account opening kit and e-mails/letters.

sections.title: Exchange and SEBI level: SCORES and SCORES 2.0

blocks.text: If unhappy with the broker, the investor can go to the exchange or SEBI. SEBI's SCORES (SEBI Complaints Redress System) is a web-based, centralised, 24x7 system for complaints against listed companies and registered intermediaries: one central database, online movement of complaints to entities, online upload of Action Taken Reports (ATRs) and real-time status tracking.

Investors register on SCORES and get an e-mail acknowledgement. A paper complaint is digitised by SEBI and uploaded; follow-up is electronic only. SEBI-recognised Investor Associations and SEBI's toll-free helpline help investors file.
Taking the grievance to the entity first is mandatory. Only if the entity fails to redress it in time can the investor use SCORES.
Revised framework (SEBI circular, September 20, 2023), which also linked SCORES to ODR:

items.title: Auto-forward
items.text: The complaint goes automatically to the entity.

items.title: ATR in 21 days
items.text: The entity resolves it and uploads an ATR within 21 calendar days; it is auto-routed to the complainant. The Designated Body (for a broker, the stock exchange) ensures timely ATRs.

items.title: First review
items.text: Complainant seeks review within 15 calendar days of the ATR. The Designated Body may seek clarification from the entity and submits a revised ATR within 10 calendar days.

items.title: Second review
items.text: Within 15 calendar days of the Designated Body's ATR. SEBI may take cognizance if the complainant is unhappy, or the Designated Body missed its 10 days.

items.title: Closure
items.text: Satisfied, or no review sought in 15 days: disposed. A second-review complaint closes only when SEBI disposes/closes it, not on mere filing of an ATR.

blocks.text: Time limit. The limitation for an arbitration reference with exchanges is three years; a SCORES complaint must be lodged within one year of the cause of action, where the entity rejected the complaint, did not respond, or the reply was unsatisfactory. SEBI may reject complaints older than one year or not first taken to the entity. Status is tracked with a unique complaint registration number; every complaint has an audit trail.
ODR or civil remedies can be used at any time; if chosen while a complaint is pending on SCORES, the SCORES complaint is treated as disposed.

items.title: Not dealt through SCORES
points: Unlisted/delisted companies, or those on the dissemination board
Sub-judice matters (court or quasi-judicial)
Other regulators (RBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, CCI) or ministries (MCA)
Sick companies, or moratorium in winding up/insolvency
Companies struck off by RoC / vanishing companies; under liquidation/BIFR
Disputes pending with the ODR mechanism of MIIs

items.title: Not a 'complaint' at all
points: Not about securities market investment
Anonymous (whistleblowers excepted); incomplete; no supporting documents
Suggestions or requests for guidance
Unhappy with a share's trading price
Non-listing of private offer shares; private agreement disputes
Fake/forged documents; outside SEBI's purview; unregulated activity

blocks.text: The workbook also retains an older one-time 'Review' option: within 15 days of closure on SCORES, escalated to the supervising official of the SEBI dealing officer. SCORES 2.0 has turned this into the two-level review above; the investor's window is 15 days either way.
Exchanges, depositories and clearing corporations must show on their website and app home pages a link to lodge complaints with them and a link to SCORES / its app.
SCORES 2.0, effective April 01, 2024 (https://scores.sebi.gov.in), is the only version for lodging complaints from that date. Its features:

items: Uniform 21 calendar day timeline across the market
Auto-routing to the entity and auto-escalation when the entity or Designated Body misses its timeline
Monitoring by Designated Bodies
Two-level review: Designated Body first, SEBI second
KRA database integration for easy registration

blocks.text: One year to lodge on SCORES versus three years limitation for arbitration with exchanges. Do not swap them.

SEBI's circular of December 03, 1997 requires every exchange to maintain at least one ISC for counselling and basic facilities. ISCs are mandatory in the four metros (New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata); exchanges with nationwide terminals also open them in 12 cities: Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Kanpur, Indore, Bangalore, Pune, Jaipur, Ghaziabad, Lucknow, Gurgaon, Patna and Vadodara. More can be opened wherever required, and an ISC can be run by one exchange or jointly by two or more.

items: Four financial dailies, at least one in the regional language
Internet-connected computer to access SEBI and exchange grievance portals
Complaints accepted in physical and electronic form; facilitation desks for dispute resolution
Arbitration and appellate arbitration facility with video-calling for online hearings
Meeting room for at least 5-6 persons plus seating for 5-6 more
Library of laws and investor material (copies at minimal cost); visitor register; phone, photocopier, printer, scanner

blocks.text: ISC staff must be trained in market operations, grievance resolution and SCORES. The Investor Charter for Stock Exchanges (modified May 2024 for ODR and SCORES 2.0) adds investor responsibilities and a code of conduct for exchanges. Complaints reach an exchange via SCORES 2.0 (exchange first review, SEBI second), the exchange's web portal, designated e-mail IDs, or SMART ODR.
Picture an ISC: 4 newspapers on the rack (one regional), a 5-6 seat meeting room, and a laptop for video-calling the arbitrator.

SEBI set up a common ODR Portal (SMART ODR) that resolves disputes with listed companies, intermediaries and MIIs through online conciliation and online arbitration. Why? A retail investor fighting a broker in court could wait years; ODR fixes a short timetable and lets everyone join by video.

items.title: Market Participant
items.text: Investor first complains to the broker/intermediary/company.

items.title: SCORES or ODR
items.text: If unhappy, escalate on SCORES, or file on SMART ODR.

items.title: MII review: 21 days
items.text: The exchange/depository tries to resolve it amicably.

items.title: Conciliation: 21 + 10 days
items.text: A conciliator attempts settlement; 10-day extension with consent.

items.title: Arbitration: 30 + 30 days
items.text: If conciliation fails, the investor may seek arbitration.

items.title: Section 34
items.text: A dissatisfied party may challenge the award under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

blocks.text: Review 21, Reconcile 21 (+10), Rule 30 (+30). Talk first, mediate second, decide last.

Disputes between investors/clients and listed companies (including RTAs) or specified intermediaries/regulated entities are resolved online. Either side, including nominees/transmission holders, may also refer unresolved service-related complaints (delayed statements or bills, account freezing, unexplained debits, branch closed without notice, demat account transferred without permission, etc.).

Specified entities: AIF managers, Bankers to an Issue and SCSBs, CIS managers, commodity clearing corporations, DPs, Investment Advisers, InvIT and REIT managers, Merchant Bankers, Mutual Funds (AMCs), Portfolio Managers, RTAs, Research Analysts and stock brokers (including Online Bond Platforms).

items.title: Retail investor
points: Uses SEBI's ODR route (SMART ODR)
Seat: where the investor permanently resides

items.title: Institutional/corporate client
points: Option: SEBI's ODR route, OR any independent institutional mediation/conciliation/arbitration in India
Seat and venue in India; may be online

blocks.text: Contractual disputes between MIIs and their constituents will be added later; disputes over MIIs' regulatory/enforcement role are excluded.

An ODR Institution runs the actual conciliation and arbitration. Each MII empanels one or more, after collecting its registration, constitution, conciliation/arbitration rules, PAN, LEI, board composition, shareholders and authorised signatories. It must be a member of the association of MII-empanelled ODR Institutions.
An MII's primary/first ODR Institution cannot be the primary/first ODR Institution of any other MII.

items: The MIIs jointly establish and operate the portal with their ODR Institutions, sharing costs under an inter-MII agreement.
SEBI inspects it from time to time.
ODR Institutions must do time-bound online conciliation/arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
The portal connects with SCORES / SEBI Intermediary portal.
All market participants must enroll within SEBI's timeline, after which they are deemed enrolled.

blocks.text: Normal route: complain to the Market Participant, then SCORES, then ODR. Alternatively, ODR can be started once the Market Participant fails to resolve it, or at any stage of the SCORES escalation. The one prerequisite: the complaint must first go to the intermediary.
The relevant MII reviews the ODR complaint and tries to resolve it within 21 days; if not, it goes to conciliation.
A Market Participant may also start ODR, after giving the investor at least 15 calendar days' notice.

The portal enrolls parties, accepts complaints and documents, and shows status updates from ODR Institutions. Typical documents: a statement of the dispute (delivery-based and squared-off trades shown separately), contract notes, bills, broker's account statement, share delivery records, margin statement, Member Constituent Agreement, Risk Disclosure Document, PAN/GIR number, balance sheet showing dues, latest ITR acknowledgement, and a list of documents.
Disputes are allotted to empanelled ODR Institutions on a market-wide round-robin basis, after the MII's review (concluded within 21 calendar days).

items.title: Appoint
items.text: The ODR Institution appoints a sole, independent, neutral conciliator within 5 days of the reference.

items.title: Settle
items.text: Meetings aim at settlement within 21 calendar days of appointment, extendable by max 10 calendar days with the parties' recorded consent.

items.title: Success
items.text: A settlement agreement, executed and stamped online.

items.title: Failure
items.text: The conciliator fixes the admissible claim value payable to the investor and notifies parties, ODR Institution and MII.

items.title: Next
items.text: The investor may go to online arbitration, run by the same ODR Institution. A Market Participant wanting arbitration must first deposit 100% of the admissible claim value with the MII.

blocks.text: A Market Participant that does not deposit cannot initiate arbitration and may face exchange action. On the investor's application, the MII may release up to ₹5,00,000 from the deposit, against an undertaking/indemnity/security to refund it if the investor loses.

Meena claims ₹8 lakh. Conciliation fails; the admissible claim is fixed at ₹6 lakh. Her broker wants arbitration, so it deposits ₹6 lakh with the exchange. Meena can get up to ₹5 lakh released now, on an undertaking to refund if she loses.
blocks.title: The ₹5 lakh release

blocks.text: ₹5 lakh caps the interim release to the investor; ₹30 lakh is the sole-arbitrator limit; ₹1 lakh is the document-only limit.

Conciliation fees may be borne by the MIIs and recovered from the Market Participant complained against; if the Market Participant starts the dispute, it pays directly. Fees can never be shifted to the investor. Conciliation is unsuccessful if no settlement is reached within the stipulated (or extended) time.
Late fee: conciliation started more than six months after the transaction/dispute costs ₹1,000, paid by the initiator (investor or Market Participant), collected by MIIs.

Arbitration is a quasi-judicial alternate dispute resolution mechanism under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, meant to give quicker resolution than courts. After failed conciliation, the investor starts online arbitration by paying fees, and the broker must participate.

head: Who starts arbitration
Broker must
rows: Deposit 100% of admissible claim with the MII and pay fees within 10 days
Inform the ODR Institution within 10 days of conciliation ending; deposit full claim within a further 5 days

head: Claim / counter-claim
Arbitrator(s)
Process
Award
rows: 30 days; may extend up to 30 more (recorded reasons)
30 days; may extend up to 30 more (recorded reasons)
blocks.caption: Arbitration by claim size

blocks.text: A non-cooperating party can face an ex-parte order after 7 calendar days' notice. Arbitrators may grant interim relief after hearing the parties; parties may seek correction of the award under the Act.

items.title: Pay
items.text: The Market Participant pays within 15 calendar days of the award (unless sooner). The MII helps the investor enforce it.

items.title: Signal a challenge
items.text: The losing party files its intention to challenge under Section 34 within 7 calendar days on the ODR Portal.

items.title: Deposit to challenge
items.text: A Market Participant must deposit 100% of the award amount with the MII before challenging.

items.title: Stay or comply
items.text: No stay within 3 months of receipt of the award means full compliance. The MII monitors compliance.

blocks.text: After the award: 7 days to say 'I'll challenge', 15 days to pay, 3 months to get a stay. A broker never fights for free: 100% deposit before arbitration, 100% before a challenge.

Sole arbitrator up to ₹30 lakh, not ₹5, 20 or 50 lakh. The ODR flow summary says the 30-day arbitration period is extendable by 30 days with the parties' consent; the detailed rule lets the arbitrator extend for recorded reasons. The numbers (30 + 30) are what get tested.
Proceedings are online (audio-video). Investors may join from the ISC of any MII.

head: Dispute
Deemed seat and venue
rows: Where the investor resides permanently (non-individual: registered office/principal place of business in India per KYC)
Client's registered/principal place in India; if none in India, the intermediary's; or a competent court in India they agree on

blocks.text: Fees depend on the claim amount, with separate fees for the arbitrator and the ODR Institution, collected by the ODR Institution.

head: Delay
Late fee
rows: Arbitration started after 1 month and up to 6 months from failed conciliation
Arbitration started after 6 months by a Market Participant
Additional 50% of fees per extra month, non-refundable
Conciliation started over 6 months after the dispute

items: All client agreements are deemed amended to include online conciliation/arbitration via the ODR Portal.
Attend promptly to complaints; communications must tell investors about SCORES and the ODR Portal.
Train staff for complaints, SCORES/ODR references and online proceedings; cooperate with MIIs and ODR Institutions.
SEBI may require an interest-free deposit with MIIs/Designated Body to honour awards or amounts payable pending arbitration or challenge.

sections.title: Broker default and the Investor Protection Fund

items.title: Declare
items.text: Exchange issues a circular declaring the broker a defaulter and posts it on its website.

items.title: Invite claims
items.text: A public notice invites claims within a specified period.

items.title: Reach clients
items.text: Clients are informed by e-mail and SMS to lodge claims.

items.title: Sanction
items.text: Claims go to the Member Committee for sanction and ratification.

items.title: Pay
items.text: The IPF Trust disburses, up to the maximum fixed for a single claim.

blocks.text: The exchange website carries eligibility norms, claim form, FAQs, online claim status, SOP and claim-processing policy, and the list of defaulter/expelled TMs. Exchanges, depositories and clearing corporations also disclose complaints received against them by the 7th of the succeeding month.

The Central Government, by notification of August 22, 1985, required exchanges to set up an IPF (also called Customer Protection Fund). It pays legitimate, non-speculative claims of clients of members declared defaulters or expelled, and is administered by a Trust. SEBI's comprehensive guidelines (May 2023) require all exchanges and depositories to have an IPF, each through a separate trust.

head: Exchange's contribution to IPF
Amount
rows: Interest on the issuer's 1% security deposit (public issue)
Penalties: client code modification; call-auction pay-in default; LODR non-compliance by listed companies
Penalty on investor pay-in default in OFS

items: Use: claims of clients of defaulting TMs and interim relief to investors.
Income: at least 70% ploughed back; 25% may fund investor education/awareness.
Review: corpus adequacy half-yearly (end March and September).
Eligible: claims within the specified period, including clients who dealt through the defaulter's registered authorised persons. Speculative claims excluded.
Late: claims more than three years after the specified period ends may be treated as a civil dispute.
Limits: per-investor compensation fixed by the exchange with the IPF Trust and SEBI.
Disclosure: IPF corpus on the website, updated monthly.
No double pay: exchanges share data on clients of defaulter members within 10 days of disablement, and PAN, UCC and amount when paying.

blocks.text: IPF income: 70 back, 25 to teach.
IPF does not cover speculative claims, but does cover clients who dealt via the defaulter's registered AP.

Exchanges set aside at least 20% of listing fees for the ISF, supervised by the Regulatory Oversight Committee. It can be used only for investor education and awareness: seminars, workshops, publications, training.

points: Compensates clients of defaulting/expelled members
1% of listing fees (quarterly)
Run by an IPF Trust

items.title: ISF
points: Investor education and awareness only
At least 20% of listing fees
Supervised by the Regulatory Oversight Committee

flashcards.q: Who is the 'backbone' of the securities market?
flashcards.a: Investors.

flashcards.q: Two kinds of party an investor may have a grievance against?
flashcards.a: (a) The intermediary/broking firm they trade through; (b) the company in which they hold shares.

flashcards.q: Three levels at which grievances are handled?
flashcards.a: Trading member (broker) level, stock exchange level, and regulator (SEBI/SCORES) level.

flashcards.q: Within how many days should a broker redress an investor complaint?
flashcards.a: 21 calendar days from receipt of the complaint.

flashcards.q: What is Exhibit 7.1?
flashcards.a: The standard notice every broker/AP office displays: compliance officer, CEO/partner, exchange/depository contacts, SCORES and SEBI helpline.

flashcards.q: By when must brokers publish monthly complaint data on their website?
flashcards.a: By the 7th of the succeeding month, in SEBI's format.

flashcards.q: What does SCORES stand for?
flashcards.a: SEBI Complaints Redress System: a 24x7 web-based centralised system for complaints against listed companies and registered intermediaries.

flashcards.q: What is an ATR?
flashcards.a: Action Taken Report: the entity's response uploaded on SCORES, due within 21 calendar days.

flashcards.q: Who is the Designated Body on SCORES for a stock broker?
flashcards.a: The stock exchange.

flashcards.q: Window to seek first review on SCORES?
flashcards.a: 15 calendar days from the date of the entity's ATR.

flashcards.q: How fast must the Designated Body give a revised ATR?
flashcards.a: Within 10 calendar days of the review being sought.

flashcards.q: Time limit to lodge a complaint on SCORES?
flashcards.a: Within one year from the date of cause of action (after first approaching the entity).

flashcards.q: What happens to a SCORES complaint if the investor opts for ODR meanwhile?
flashcards.a: It is treated as disposed on SCORES.

flashcards.q: When did SCORES 2.0 start?
flashcards.a: April 01, 2024 (https://scores.sebi.gov.in).

flashcards.q: Name four SCORES 2.0 features.
flashcards.a: Uniform 21-day timeline, auto-routing, auto-escalation, two-level review (Designated Body then SEBI), KRA integration, Designated Body monitoring.

flashcards.q: Can SCORES take a sub-judice complaint?
flashcards.a: No. Matters before courts or quasi-judicial bodies are not dealt with through SCORES.

flashcards.q: Minimum ISCs per exchange, and the four metros?
flashcards.a: At least one; New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

flashcards.q: How many financial newspapers must an ISC keep?
flashcards.a: Four, at least one in the regional language.

flashcards.q: Who runs the conciliation/arbitration under SMART ODR?
flashcards.a: The ODR Institution empanelled by an MII; it also administers the online arbitration.

flashcards.q: How are disputes allocated among ODR Institutions?
flashcards.a: Market-wide round-robin, after the MII's 21-day review.

flashcards.q: Conciliation timeline under ODR?
flashcards.a: 21 calendar days from conciliator's appointment, extendable by max 10 calendar days with parties' consent.

flashcards.q: Within how many days is the conciliator appointed?
flashcards.a: Within 5 days of the ODR Institution receiving the reference.

flashcards.q: Notice a Market Participant must give before starting ODR?
flashcards.a: At least 15 calendar days to the investor/client.

flashcards.q: Maximum the MII may release to the investor from the MP's deposit?
flashcards.a: ₹5,00,000, against an undertaking/indemnity/security to return it if the investor loses.

flashcards.q: Late fee for starting conciliation after six months?
flashcards.a: ₹1,000, paid by whoever initiates (investor or Market Participant).

flashcards.q: Sole arbitrator vs tribunal threshold?
flashcards.a: Up to ₹30 lakh: sole arbitrator. Above ₹30 lakh: tribunal of three arbitrators.

flashcards.q: When is arbitration document-only?
flashcards.a: When the claim/counter-claim is ₹1 lakh or below; hearing only for recorded reasons.

flashcards.q: Time to pass the arbitral award?
flashcards.a: 30 calendar days from appointment, extendable by up to 30 more.

flashcards.q: Deadline for MP to pay an arbitral award?
flashcards.a: 15 calendar days from the award (unless the award says sooner).

flashcards.q: Deadline to declare intention to challenge an award u/s 34?
flashcards.a: 7 calendar days, on the ODR Portal.

flashcards.q: Who established the IPF requirement, and when?
flashcards.a: Central Government notification dated August 22, 1985.

flashcards.q: Share of listing fees to IPF vs ISF?
flashcards.a: IPF: 1% (quarterly). ISF: at least 20%.

flashcards.q: What share of IPF income must go back into the IPF?
flashcards.a: At least 70%; 25% may be used for investor education and awareness.

flashcards.q: Are speculative-transaction claims paid from IPF?
flashcards.a: No. Only legitimate, non-speculative claims of clients of defaulting/expelled members.

flashcards.q: Who sanctions claims against a defaulter before IPF Trust pays?
flashcards.a: The Member Committee (MC), for sanction and ratification.

flashcards.q: Who supervises the Investor Services Fund?
flashcards.a: The Regulatory Oversight Committee of the exchange.

questions.q: According to the workbook, who is the backbone of the securities market?
questions.why: The chapter opens by stating that investors are the backbone of the securities market; everything else exists to serve and protect them.

questions.q: Arbitration, as an alternate dispute resolution mechanism, aims at what kind of legal resolution of disputes?
questions.why: Arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is an alternative to courts meant to resolve disputes faster; ODR awards are due within 30 days.

questions.q: Under the ODR framework, claims up to what amount are decided by a sole arbitrator?
questions.why: Claims up to ₹30 lakh go to a sole independent arbitrator; above ₹30 lakh, a three-member arbitral tribunal hears the matter.

questions.q: The Investor Protection Fund that compensates clients of a defaulting trading member is established and maintained by:
questions.why: The IPF is established and maintained by the exchange (administered through a trust) to meet legitimate claims of clients of defaulting or expelled members.

questions.q: Online arbitration under SMART ODR is administered by:
questions.why: Online arbitration is administered by the ODR Institution that also facilitated the conciliation.

questions.q: Within how many days from receipt of a complaint is a stock broker expected to redress an investor grievance?
questions.why: Both the broker's obligation and the Investor Charter state 21 calendar days from receipt of the complaint.

questions.q: An investor wants to complain on SCORES about a broker's action. Within what period from the date of cause of action should the complaint be lodged?
questions.why: SCORES complaints may be lodged within one year of the cause of action; three years is the limitation for an arbitration reference with exchanges.

questions.q: The broker uploads an ATR on SCORES, but the complainant is not satisfied. Within how many days of the ATR may the complainant seek the first review?
questions.why: First review must be sought within 15 calendar days from the date of the ATR; the Designated Body then has 10 calendar days to submit a revised ATR.

questions.q: For a complaint against a stock broker on SCORES 2.0, who carries out the first review?
questions.why: The stock exchange is the Designated Body for stock brokers and does the first review; SEBI does the second review.

questions.q: An investor must first take up the grievance with the broker before filing on SCORES or SMART ODR.
questions.why: It is mandatory to approach the entity first; only if it fails to redress the grievance can the investor go to SCORES or ODR.

questions.q: Which of the following complaints is NOT dealt with through SCORES?
options: Non-receipt of contract notes from a broker
A matter already under consideration by a court of law
Delay in credit of shares by a depository participant
Non-receipt of a dividend from a listed company
questions.why: Sub-judice complaints, i.e. those under consideration by a court or quasi-judicial body, are excluded from SCORES.

questions.q: A complaint is pending on SCORES and the investor files the same dispute on SMART ODR. What happens to the SCORES complaint?
options: It is kept pending until the ODR award
It is transferred to SEBI's second review
It is treated as disposed on SCORES
It is rejected as a duplicate and the ODR filing is also cancelled
questions.why: Investors may opt for ODR or civil remedies at any time; if they do so while a complaint is pending on SCORES, it is treated as disposed on SCORES.

questions.q: SCORES 2.0, with auto-routing, auto-escalation and a two-level review, came into effect from:
questions.why: SCORES 2.0 was launched with effect from April 01, 2024; complaints can be lodged only on the new version from that date.

questions.q: Under SMART ODR, the conciliator must try to settle the dispute within 21 calendar days of appointment. By how much can this be extended?
options: A maximum of 10 calendar days, with the consent of the parties
A maximum of 21 calendar days, at the conciliator's discretion
questions.why: The 21-day conciliation period can be extended by a maximum of 10 calendar days by consent of the disputing parties, recorded in writing or electronically.

questions.q: Within how many days of receiving a reference must the ODR Institution appoint the conciliator?
questions.why: The ODR Institution appoints a sole independent conciliator within 5 days of receipt of the reference.

questions.q: Conciliation fails and the broker wants to go for arbitration. What must the broker do first?
options: Deposit 100% of the admissible claim value with the relevant MII
Deposit 50% of the claim with the ODR Institution
questions.why: A Market Participant wishing to pursue arbitration must deposit 100% of the admissible claim value with the MII before initiating it; otherwise it cannot initiate arbitration.

questions.q: From the broker's deposit of the admissible claim value, the MII may release to the investor, on application, an amount not exceeding:
questions.why: The MII may release up to ₹5,00,000 to the investor after taking an undertaking/indemnity/security for return if the arbitration goes against the investor.

questions.q: An investor's claim against a broker in ODR arbitration is ₹80,000. How will the arbitration normally proceed?
options: Hearings before a sole arbitrator, award in 60 days
Document-only arbitration by a sole arbitrator, award within 30 calendar days
It goes back to SCORES because it is below ₹1 lakh
questions.why: For claims of ₹1 lakh or below, the sole arbitrator conducts a document-only process and passes the award within 30 calendar days; a hearing can be granted only for recorded reasons.

questions.q: A client's claim against a broker is ₹45 lakh. Who will decide it in ODR arbitration?
options: An arbitral tribunal of three arbitrators
The Member Committee of the exchange
questions.why: Claims above ₹30 lakh are decided by an arbitral tribunal of three arbitrators.

questions.q: An arbitral award directs a broker to pay the investor. Unless the award requires earlier payment, within how many days must the broker pay?
questions.why: The Market Participant must pay within 15 calendar days of the arbitral award, unless the award requires payment sooner.

questions.q: The party against whom an arbitral award is passed must notify its intention to challenge the award under Section 34 within:
options: 7 calendar days, on the ODR Portal
questions.why: The intention to challenge under Section 34 must be submitted within 7 calendar days on the ODR Portal; if no stay is granted within 3 months, the award must be complied with fully.

questions.q: A broker wants to start ODR proceedings against a client over unpaid dues. What is required before it can do so?
options: A deposit of ₹5 lakh with the exchange
At least 15 calendar days' notice to the client to resolve the dispute
questions.why: A Market Participant may initiate ODR only after giving the investor at least 15 calendar days' notice for resolving the dispute.

questions.q: Where is the seat of an online arbitration between an individual investor and a stock broker deemed to be?
options: Where the broker has its registered office
Where the ODR Institution is located
Mumbai, where SEBI's head office is
questions.why: For investor-vs-intermediary disputes, the venue and seat is where the investor permanently resides (for non-individuals, the registered/principal place of business in India per KYC).

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct contribution by a stock exchange to its Investor Protection Fund?
options: 1% of listing fees, on a quarterly basis
100% of the security deposit kept by issuers
questions.why: Exchanges contribute 1% of listing fees quarterly to the IPF; 20% of listing fees goes to the Investor Services Fund, and it is 100% of the interest (not the deposit) on the issuer's 1% security deposit.

questions.q: A client's claim against a defaulter broker arises from speculative transactions. It is eligible for compensation from the IPF.
questions.why: Claims arising out of speculative transactions are not eligible for compensation from the IPF.

questions.q: At least what share of the yearly interest/income from IPF investments must be ploughed back into the IPF?
questions.why: At least 70% of IPF income is ploughed back into the fund; 25% can be used for investor education and awareness.
